walkthroughs.body_html: The Grain Procurement Crisis of 1927-28 prompted Stalin to abandon the New Economic Policy in favour of forced industrialisation and collectivisation. The First Five-Year Plan (1928-32) prioritised heavy industry — coal, steel, electricity and machinery — and unrealistic targets were often 'achieved' on paper.

Collectivisation provoked fierce peasant resistance. Slaughter of livestock and resistance to grain procurement met with arrests, deportations and executions of 'kulaks'. The catastrophic famine of 1932-33, especially in Ukraine (the Holodomor), killed several million people and is recognised by many states as genocide.

Industrial output expanded rapidly: cities such as Magnitogorsk and Stalingrad grew dramatically. Stakhanovite campaigns from 1935 promoted heroic worker productivity. By the late 1930s the USSR ranked among the world's leading industrial economies, providing the base that would resist Nazi invasion — though at enormous human cost.
